title: India's IT Giants Face Their Most Scrutinised Earnings Season in Years — and AI Is the Elephant in Every Boardroom
excerpt: With the Nifty IT index down 33% from its February peak, TCS and Infosys are about to report June-quarter results that could determine whether the sector's correction is a buying opportunity or the start of a structural decline.
body:
India's $250-billion IT services sector is heading into what may be the most consequential earnings season in a decade. Starting with Tata Consultancy Services on July 9, followed by Infosys on July 23, the country's largest software exporters will report their June-quarter (Q1 FY27) results into a market that has turned deeply sceptical about their future.

The numbers themselves are expected to be unremarkable. Emkay Global Financial Services projects constant-currency revenue growth across the top five IT firms — TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra — to range from a decline of 1.5 percent to growth of just 2 percent. Margins will be squeezed by annual wage hikes even as a weaker rupee provides some cushion. What will matter far more than the quarterly prints is what management teams say about the road ahead.

A Sector Under Pressure

The Nifty IT index has corrected more than 33 percent from its February 2026 peak, making IT the worst-performing sector on the Indian market this year. The decline reflects a confluence of pressures that have been building for over two years.

Discretionary technology spending — the project-based work that drives incremental revenue growth — remains stubbornly weak as global enterprises delay decisions amid macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty. Deal cycles have lengthened. Budgets that were once earmarked for large digital transformation projects are being diverted toward AI experimentation, often at the expense of traditional outsourcing contracts.

JP Morgan recently downgraded both HCLTech and Wipro to Underweight, while retaining Overweight ratings on Infosys and TCS. The brokerage expects the typical first-half recovery for Indian IT companies to fail this year, citing delayed deal closures, slower project ramp-ups and cautious enterprise spending.

The AI Question

Artificial intelligence has become the single biggest factor shaping investor sentiment toward the sector. The question is no longer whether AI will affect Indian IT — it already has. HCLTech has become the first major player to quantify the impact, estimating 3 to 5 percent pricing erosion across the industry as clients demand that AI-driven productivity gains be passed through to contract pricing.

Research from 360 ONE Capital notes that the latest generation of large language models — GPT, Claude, Gemini — can now generate, review, debug and explain code with increasing sophistication, directly challenging the industry's core business model of billing clients based on engineering hours. Clients are increasingly demanding those efficiency gains immediately, rather than allowing vendors to retain them as margin.

Yet most analysts stop short of calling AI an existential threat. Guggenheim Securities recently argued that software valuations are pricing in the assumption that many companies will decline indefinitely because of AI — an assumption it called "disconnected from reality." The brokerage upgraded several global software firms, arguing that enterprises will continue needing consulting, implementation, integration and cybersecurity support regardless of how AI evolves.

For Indian IT specifically, the transition appears more evolutionary than catastrophic. Companies that adapt their business models — moving from headcount-based billing to outcome-based pricing, building proprietary AI platforms and embedding AI capabilities into client engagements — are likely to survive and potentially thrive. Those that cling to the old model will face sustained margin pressure.

What to Watch

Three things will determine whether the sector's correction represents a buying opportunity or a value trap.

Guidance revisions are the most important signal. Infosys is expected to raise its FY27 constant-currency revenue growth guidance to 2–4 percent from 1.5–3.5 percent, reflecting contributions from its recent Stratus and Optimum acquisitions. HCLTech may trim its services growth outlook to 1–3.5 percent. The gap between these two narratives — Infosys buying growth through M&A while HCLTech faces organic headwinds — will tell investors whether the recovery is broad-based or isolated.

BFSI commentary matters because banking and financial services remains the most resilient vertical. If even BFSI spending shows signs of softening, the near-term outlook becomes significantly worse.

AI monetisation evidence is the wild card. Companies that can point to new revenue streams generated by AI — not just cost savings — will command a premium. Those that cannot will continue to face valuation compression.

The NRI Investor Angle

For diaspora investors with exposure to Indian IT, the earnings season presents a genuine fork in the road. Tier-1 IT companies are now trading roughly 30 to 40 percent below their long-term average price-to-earnings multiples, according to Motilal Oswal. That kind of valuation discount is historically rare for India's most reliable earnings compounders.

But valuations alone have never been sufficient to drive re-rating in Indian IT. The sector needs evidence that enterprise demand is stabilising, pricing pressure is manageable, and AI is creating new opportunities faster than it is cannibalising existing ones. Until those signals emerge, investors should expect the sector to oscillate between relief rallies triggered by value buying and fresh selloffs driven by weak earnings and cautious commentary.

The next three weeks will provide the clearest answer yet.
